blocks.cap: Look at how the two trees begin in completely different ways. On the left we first cut 72 into 8 and 9, while on the right we first cut it into 6 and 12, and along the way that 12 even splits again through a 4. Yet no matter which first cut you choose, both trees funnel all the way down to the same atoms, namely two, two, two, three, three. That shared fingerprint is \(2^3 \times 3^2\), and it shows the uniqueness from the key idea above, since every honest factor tree for 72 has to land on exactly this collection of primes.

blocks.x: A craftsperson has 360 beads (\(360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5\)) and wants a perfect square total. What is the smallest whole number to multiply 360 by so that the result is a perfect square?
hints: Look at the fingerprint \(360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5\). When you build a square of side \(s\), each side gets exactly half of every prime in the total. So think about which exponents can be split into two equal whole pieces and which cannot.

An exponent like the 2 on the \(3\) splits evenly into \(1\) and \(1\). But the 3 on the \(2\) and the hidden 1 on the \(5\) are odd, so they cannot be cut cleanly in half. Each odd exponent is the real problem.
To turn an odd exponent into an even one, you only need one more copy of that prime. Find every prime with an odd exponent, and multiply by exactly one of each. Then ask what that product is.
blocks.sol:
$$360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$$

A perfect square needs every exponent even. The \(3^2\) is already fine, but \(2^3\) needs one more 2 and \(5^1\) needs one more 5, so multiply by \(2 \times 5 = 10\). That gives \(360 \times 10 = 3600 = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 = 60^2\), so the smallest multiplier is \(\boxed{10}\).

Halving each exponent gives the side length, \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60\), and halving only works when every exponent is even.

blocks.x: A toy company has 144 cubes (\(144 = 2^4 \times 3^2\)). What is the smallest positive whole number to multiply 144 by so the result is a perfect cube?
hints: A perfect square wanted every prime to show up an even number of times so it could split into two equal groups. A perfect cube splits into three equal groups instead. How many times must each prime appear so it can be shared evenly among three layers?

Look at the fingerprint \(2^4 \times 3^2\). For a cube, each exponent has to be a multiple of \(3\). The exponent \(4\) is not a multiple of \(3\), and neither is \(2\). Climb each one up to the next multiple of \(3\).

The next multiple of \(3\) above \(4\) is \(6\), so you are short two \(2\)s. The next multiple of \(3\) above \(2\) is \(3\), so you are short one \(3\). Multiply those missing primes together to find your number.
blocks.sol:
$$144 = 2^4 \times 3^2$$

A perfect cube needs every exponent to be a multiple of 3. The exponent 4 has to climb to 6, costing two more 2s, and the exponent 2 has to climb to 3, costing one more 3. So multiply by

$$2^2 \times 3 = 12,$$

which gives \(144 \times 12 = 2^6 \times 3^3 = 12^3 = 1728\). The answer is \(\boxed{12}\).

A square splits the primes into two equal groups and a cube into three, which is why the test moves from even exponents to multiples of 3.

blocks.x: Read the prime fingerprint and look only at the exponents. It is a perfect square exactly when every exponent is even, since the square root halves each one, and a perfect cube exactly when every exponent is a multiple of 3, since the cube root takes a third of each. Both are one idea. A number is a perfect $k$-th power exactly when every exponent is divisible by $k$. To reach the nearest square or cube, top up each short exponent with the missing copies of that prime.
The hidden number has fingerprint \(2^4 \times 3 \times 5^6\). Each trailing zero needs one 2 paired with one 5. How many zeros does the number end in?
hints: A number ends in a zero exactly when it is divisible by \(10\). What two prime building blocks does \(10\) split into?
Since \(10 = 2 \times 5\), every trailing zero comes from one factor of \(2\) teamed up with one factor of \(5\). So count how many such teams you can make.
You have four \(2\)s and six \(5\)s. Pair them off one for one. The moment you run out of the scarcer prime, you cannot form any more complete \(2\)-and-\(5\) teams.
blocks.sol:
Each trailing zero is a factor of \(10 = 2 \times 5\), so it costs one 2 paired with one 5. The fingerprint \(2^4 \times 3 \times 5^6\) holds four 2s and six 5s, so you can build four pairs before the 2s run out. The number ends in \(\boxed{4}\) zeros.

The scarcer prime sets the count. Two spare 5s are left with no partner, and a lone 5 cannot make a zero.

blocks.x: Find the smallest perfect square divisible by 2, 3, 5, and 7 all at once.
hints: Think in terms of the prime fingerprint of the number. For the pile to share evenly into groups of \(2\), of \(3\), of \(5\), and of \(7\), each of those primes has to appear in the fingerprint at least once.

Now bring in the perfect square idea from earlier. A number is a perfect square exactly when every exponent in its prime fingerprint is even. An odd count like one will not do, so each prime needs to show up an even number of times.

Combine the two requirements. Each of \(2, 3, 5, 7\) must appear, and each must appear an even number of times. The smallest even count that is still at least one is two, so try giving every prime an exponent of exactly \(2\) and compute the result.
blocks.sol:
Each of 2, 3, 5, and 7 has to appear in the fingerprint, and a perfect square needs every exponent even, so the smallest exponent each one can take is 2.

$$2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 \times 7^2 = (2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7)^2 = 210^2 = 44100$$

The smallest such square is \(\boxed{44100}\).

The divisibility demands set a floor on each exponent, and the square condition rounds every floor up to the next even number.

blocks.x: Primes never run out: multiply any finite list and add 1, and the result has a new prime factor. Yet primes thin out, gaps of any desired length with no prime inside can always be found.

This section leaves you with two tools. You can test whether a number is prime by dividing by the primes up to \(\sqrt{n}\), and you can read a number's prime fingerprint to get divisibility, perfect powers, and trailing zeros. Next we put two fingerprints side by side to find the GCD and LCM.

review.x: A librarian checks which of 143, 149, 151, 161, and 167 are prime. Every number here is below \(169=13^2\), so test primes up to 13. How many of the five are prime?
hints: All five are odd and none end in 0 or 5, so 2 and 5 will never divide them. That leaves only 3, 7, 11, and 13 to worry about.
Use the divisibility tests from section 3.2 to clear out 3 quickly, then test the survivors against 7, 11, and 13 by actual division.
Two of the five hide a factor. Try \(143 = 11 \times 13\) and look for a number that is \(7 \times 23\). The other three resist every prime up to 13.
review.sol:
All five are odd and none end in 0 or 5, and the digit sums 8, 14, 7, 8, 14 rule out 3. That leaves 7, 11, and 13 to test.

$$143 = 11 \times 13, \qquad 161 = 7 \times 23$$

Those two are composite. 149, 151, and 167 leave a remainder against 7, 11, and 13, and since all five sit below \(169 = 13^2\), there is nothing further to check. So \(\boxed{3}\) of the five are prime.

Trial division can stop at \(\sqrt{n}\), because any factor above it already comes with a smaller partner below it.

review.x: Find the largest two-digit prime whose tens digit and units digit are both composite.
hints: First figure out which single digits actually count as composite. Check each digit from \(1\) to \(9\) and ask whether it has a factor other than \(1\) and itself. Only those digits are allowed in either spot.
You want the biggest number, so start as high as you can. Try a tens digit of \(9\) first, then \(8\), and for each one only allow units digits from your composite list.

When you test a candidate, use the divisibility ideas from section 3.2 to throw out numbers fast, then check the survivor against small primes like \(2\), \(3\), and \(7\) to confirm it really is prime.
review.sol:
The composite single digits are 4, 6, 8, and 9, so both digits must come from that set. Starting at the top, 99, 98, 96, and 94 are all composite, since three of them are even and \(99 = 9 \times 11\). Next comes 89. It is odd, its digit sum is 17, it does not end in 0 or 5, and 7 misses it since \(7 \times 12 = 84\) and \(7 \times 13 = 91\). With \(\sqrt{89} < 10\) that finishes the check, so the answer is \(\boxed{89}\).

The digit 1 counts as neither prime nor composite, so it is not allowed in either spot.

review.x: At a mixer, two guests pair if both ages are prime and add to 48. How many unordered prime pairs sum to 48?
hints: Pick the smaller prime in each pair and walk it upward. For each small prime \(p\), the partner has to be \(48 - p\). You only need to check whether that partner is also prime.
Since \(48\) is even, two odd primes can add to it, so you can skip past \(2\) and try the odd primes \(3, 5, 7, 11, \dots\) as the smaller one.
To avoid counting a pair twice, stop once the smaller prime passes the halfway point \(24\). Any pair you would find beyond that you have already met from the other side.
review.sol:
Let the smaller prime \(p\) climb and ask each time whether \(48 - p\) is also prime.

$$(5, 43), \qquad (7, 41), \qquad (11, 37), \qquad (17, 31), \qquad (19, 29)$$

The rest fail, since \(45\), \(35\), and \(25\) are composite, and 2 is out because \(46\) is not prime. Stopping at the halfway point 24 keeps you from counting a pair twice, so there are \(\boxed{5}\) pairs.

An even sum forces both primes to be odd, which is why 2 never shows up in any pair here.

review.x: Stickers print in runs of \(6p\) where \(p\) is prime, and the run must stay under 800. What is the largest prime bundle size \(p\)?
hints: First turn the packing limit into a ceiling on \(p\). If \(6 \times p\) must stay under 800, then \(p\) itself must stay under \(800 \div 6\). Work out that quotient before you go prime hunting.
The quotient \(800 \div 6\) is not a whole number, so \(p\) has to be at or below the largest whole number underneath it. Find that whole number first, then ask whether it is prime.

Once you have the top candidate, walk downward one number at a time and test each for primality using the divisibility tests from section 3.2. The first prime you land on is your answer. Watch out: a number ending in 1 or 3 can still be composite.
review.sol:
The run \(6p\) must stay under 800, so \(p < \tfrac{800}{6} = 133\tfrac{1}{3}\), which caps \(p\) at 133. Walking down, \(133 = 7 \times 19\) is composite and 132 is even. Then 131 survives 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11, and \(12^2 = 144 > 131\), so it is prime. The largest bundle size is \(\boxed{131}\).

A number ending in 1 or 3 can still be composite, as 133 shows, so the top candidate is worth testing rather than trusting.

review.x: Find two prime numbers that add to 39. There is exactly one pair. What is the larger prime?
hints: Is \(39\) even or odd? Now think about what happens when you add two odd numbers together, or two even numbers together.
To land on an odd total, one of your two primes has to be even and the other has to be odd. How many even prime numbers are there?
The only even prime is \(2\). If one prime must be \(2\), what is the other prime forced to be, and is that number actually prime?
review.sol:
39 is odd, so one of the two primes has to be even, and 2 is the only even prime. That forces the other to be \(39 - 2 = 37\), which is prime since 2, 3, and 5 all miss and \(6^2 = 36 < 37 < 49\). The larger prime is \(\boxed{37}\).

Whenever two primes add to an odd number, one of them must be 2, which usually pins the whole pair down at once.

review.x: How many distinct prime factors does 2310 have?
hints: Start by stripping off the smallest primes one at a time. Is 2310 even? Does the digit-sum trick from 3.2 tell you about 3? Does it end in 0 or 5?
Each time you find a prime that divides cleanly, divide it out and keep working with the smaller number that is left. Keep going until what remains is itself a prime.
Count only the *different* primes you used. If a prime never repeated, you are simply listing the distinct primes whose product is 2310.
review.sol:
Peel off the smallest prime each time. \(2310 = 2 \times 1155\), then \(1155 = 3 \times 385\), then \(385 = 5 \times 77\), and \(77 = 7 \times 11\).

$$2310 = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11$$

No prime repeats, so the number of distinct prime factors is \(\boxed{5}\).

2310 is the product of the first five primes, which is why its factorization comes out so clean.

review.x: Two tools, gathered. Test primality by dividing by primes up to \(\sqrt{n}\), and the 3.2 shortcuts clear 2, 3, 5 instantly. The fingerprint \(n=p^a q^b\cdots\) reveals divisibility, perfect squares (all exponents even), perfect cubes (all multiples of 3), and trailing zeros (2-and-5 pairs).
A box shows \(2^x \times 3^y \times 5^z = 6000\). Find \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) by factoring 6000, then enter their sum \(x+y+z\).
hints: The left side is already broken into prime building blocks. If you break 6000 into the same building blocks, the matching powers must line up. Try splitting 6000 into easier chunks first, like 6 and 1000.
Six is \(2 \times 3\), and 1000 is \(10 \times 10 \times 10\), so each thousand piece carries one \(2\) and one \(5\). Collect all the 2s together, all the 3s together, and all the 5s together.
Once 6000 is written purely as a power of 2 times a power of 3 times a power of 5, just read the three exponents straight off and add them.
review.sol:
Split 6000 into \(6 \times 1000\). Six is \(2 \times 3\), and \(1000 = 10^3 = 2^3 \times 5^3\), so

$$6000 = 2^4 \times 3^1 \times 5^3.$$

A prime factorization is unique, so the exponents on each side must agree one for one, giving \(x = 4\), \(y = 1\), \(z = 3\) and \(x + y + z = \boxed{8}\).

Uniqueness is what lets you read the exponents straight off both sides. Without it, matching prime powers would prove nothing.

review.x: A tiler has 252 tiles (\(252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7\)) and needs a perfect-square total. What is the smallest whole number to multiply 252 by?
hints: Break 252 all the way down into a product of primes. Once it is written as primes raised to powers, the key to being a perfect square lives in those exponents.
A whole number is a perfect square exactly when every prime in its factorization appears an even number of times. Look at your exponents on \(2\), \(3\), and \(7\). Which one is odd?
Only one prime has an odd exponent. You do not need to touch the others. Multiply by just enough copies of that one prime to make its exponent even.
review.sol:
$$252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7$$

Only the 7 sits at an odd exponent, so one more 7 fixes it. The smallest multiplier is \(\boxed{7}\), and \(252 \times 7 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7^2 = 42^2 = 1764\).

A perfect square has every exponent even, so you only ever multiply by the primes currently sitting at an odd exponent.

review.x: A sculptor has 72 cubes (\(72 = 2^3 \times 3^2\)) and wants a perfect-cube total. What is the smallest whole number to multiply 72 by?
hints: Break 72 into its prime factorization first. Writing it as a product of primes raised to powers will let you see the structure clearly.

A number is a perfect cube exactly when every exponent in its prime factorization is a multiple of 3, since you are splitting the factors evenly into three identical groups. Check each exponent against the nearest multiple of 3.
The exponent on 2 is already fine. Look only at the exponent on 3 and ask how many more factors of 3 you must supply to push that exponent up to the next multiple of 3.
review.sol:
$$72 = 2^3 \times 3^2$$

A perfect cube needs every exponent to be a multiple of 3. The exponent on 2 is already 3, and the exponent on 3 has to climb from 2 to 3, so one more factor of 3 does it. Multiplying by \(\boxed{3}\) gives \(2^3 \times 3^3 = 6^3 = 216\).

Nothing smaller works. Multiplying by 2 would push the exponent on 2 up to 4 and leave both exponents off a multiple of 3.

review.x: Two numbers multiply to 504. Each is divisible by 6 but neither equals 6. What is the larger of the two numbers?
hints: Since each number is divisible by \(6\), try writing the first as \(6m\) and the second as \(6n\) for some whole numbers \(m\) and \(n\). What does their product look like now?
Pulling a \(6\) out of each factor gives \(6m \times 6n = 36 \times mn\). Set that equal to \(504\) and figure out what (mn) must be.
Once you know (mn), list the factor pairs of that small number. One pair forces a number to equal \(6\), which is forbidden, so cross it out and keep the pair that survives.
review.sol:
Both numbers are divisible by 6, so write them as \(6m\) and \(6n\). Then \(36mn = 504\), which gives \(mn = 14\). The factor pairs of 14 are \(1 \times 14\) and \(2 \times 7\), and the first is out because it would make one number \(6 \times 1 = 6\). The other pair gives \(6 \times 2 = 12\) and \(6 \times 7 = 42\), so the larger is \(\boxed{42}\).

Pulling the shared factor out of both numbers shrinks 504 down to 14, which you can factor at a glance.

review.x: A rectangular garden has area 1271 sq ft with both side lengths two-digit whole numbers. There is exactly one such rectangle. What is the length of its longer side?
hints: A side length of the rectangle must be a whole number that divides 1271 evenly, so you are really hunting for a factor of 1271.
From section 3.1, remember that factor pairs cluster around the square root. Since \(\sqrt{1271}\) is a little under 36, you only need to test factors up to about 35.
Use the divisibility tests from section 3.2 to skip the easy cases, then keep testing primes. Try 7, 11, 13, and onward. One of the primes in the low 30s divides 1271 cleanly.
review.sol:
A side length has to divide 1271, and since \(35^2 = 1225\) and \(36^2 = 1296\), the smaller side is at most 35. Testing primes, 2, 3, and 5 fail on sight, then 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, and 29 all fail, and 31 divides cleanly.

$$1271 = 31 \times 41$$

Both 31 and 41 are prime, so this is the only factor pair above 1, and the longer side is \(\boxed{41}\).

When a number is a product of two primes, it has exactly one rectangle with both sides bigger than 1.

review.x: Find all sets of three different primes that add to 30. How many such sets are there?
hints: Think about even and odd, just like the parity reasoning from before. If all three primes were odd, what kind of total would you get, and does that match 30?
Since 30 is even but three odd primes give an odd sum, one of the primes has to be the only even prime there is. Which prime is that, and what must the other two add up to once you set it aside?

With one prime fixed as 2, you need two different primes that add to 28. Walk up from the smallest primes \(3, 5, 7, 11, ...\) and check which pairs of different primes total 28. Count how many such pairs you find.
review.sol:
Three odd numbers add to an odd total, but 30 is even, so one of the three primes has to be 2. The other two must add to 28.

$$28 = 5 + 23, \qquad 28 = 11 + 17$$

The other starts fail, since 25, 21, and 15 are all composite. That gives the sets \(\{2, 5, 23\}\) and \(\{2, 11, 17\}\), so the count is \(\boxed{2}\).

A parity check collapses the search before you start guessing, turning a three-number hunt into a two-number one.

review.x: Every checked even number above 2 equals two primes added together. Goldbach conjectured this holds for all even numbers, but no proof exists after nearly 300 years.

blocks.x: Two numbers raise two natural questions. What is the biggest number that divides both of them, and what is the smallest number that both of them divide? The first answer is the GCD and the second is the LCM. The prime fingerprints from 3.3 give you both.
A maker has ribbons of 56 cm and 70 cm. She wants to cut both into equal whole-centimeter pieces with no scrap. List the divisors of each and find the longest piece length that works for both.
hints: A piece length works for a ribbon only if it divides that ribbon's length with nothing left over. So write the divisors of 56 and the divisors of 70, then look for the numbers that show up on both lists.
The divisors of 56 are \(1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 14, 28, 56\) and the divisors of 70 are \(1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 14, 35, 70\). Which numbers sit on both lists, and which of those is biggest?
blocks.sol: A piece length works on a ribbon only if it divides that length evenly, so write out both divisor lists. $$56: \quad 1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 7,\ 8,\ 14,\ 28,\ 56$$ $$70: \quad 1,\ 2,\ 5,\ 10,\ 7,\ 14,\ 35,\ 70$$ The numbers on both lists are \(1, 2, 7,\) and \(14\), and the largest is \(\boxed{14}\) centimeters. That gives \(56 = 14 \times 4\) and \(70 = 14 \times 5\), four pieces from one ribbon and five from the other with no scrap.

blocks.x: Use the fingerprints \(168 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 7\) and \(180 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5\) to find \(\gcd(168, 180)\). Take each shared prime to its lower power.
hints: Go prime by prime. For the prime \(2\), the number \(168\) carries three of them and \(180\) carries two. A divisor of both can lean on at most the smaller count, two. Do the same for \(3\), and then ask whether \(5\) or \(7\) can appear at all.
A prime that lives in only one fingerprint cannot divide the other number, so it cannot appear in the gcd. Take each shared prime to the smaller of its two powers, then multiply those together.
blocks.sol: Go prime by prime and keep the smaller power. For \(2\), that is \(2^2\). For \(3\), it is \(3^1\). The \(5\) sits only in \(180\) and the \(7\) only in \(168\), so neither can divide both numbers. $$\gcd(168,180) = 2^2 \times 3 = \boxed{12}$$ A common divisor can only use primes both numbers carry, and never more copies than the smaller supply has.

blocks.x: A volunteer has 90 soap bars and 126 seed packets. Every kit holds the same counts with no leftovers. With \(\gcd(90,126)\), find the greatest number of identical kits she can build.
hints: The number of kits must divide \(90\) evenly, so the soap splits with none left over, and it must also divide \(126\) evenly for the seeds. So the kit count is a common divisor of \(90\) and \(126\), and she wants the greatest one.
Take each shared prime to its lower power. Both numbers carry \(2\), both carry \(3^2\), but \(5\) belongs only to \(90\) and \(7\) only to \(126\). Multiply the shared part.
blocks.sol: The kit count has to divide both totals evenly, so it is a common divisor of \(90\) and \(126\), and she wants the greatest one. $$90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5, \qquad 126 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7$$ Both carry one \(2\) and both carry \(3^2\), while \(5\) belongs to \(90\) alone and \(7\) to \(126\) alone. $$\gcd(90,126) = 2 \times 3^2 = \boxed{18}$$ Each kit holds \(90 \div 18 = 5\) bars and \(126 \div 18 = 7\) packets. Splitting two quantities into as many identical full shares as possible is always a gcd question.

blocks.x: The greatest common divisor gcd(a,b), also called the greatest common factor, is the largest number that divides both a and b with nothing left over. Every pair has 1 on both divisor lists, so a common divisor always exists, and since a number never has a divisor larger than itself, there is always a single greatest one. Lay two fingerprints side by side and the gcd takes each shared prime to the lower of its two powers, because a common divisor can only use primes both numbers carry, and only as many copies as the stingier number has. A prime in just one fingerprint contributes nothing. When two numbers share no prime at all, their only common divisor is 1 and we call them coprime.
Two gears have 24 and 35 teeth, with \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\) and \(35 = 5 \times 7\). They share no prime factor. How many teeth must pass the meshing point before the red teeth touch again?
hints: The red teeth realign after a count of teeth that both \(24\) and \(35\) divide evenly, so you want the smallest number that is a multiple of both. Start listing multiples of \(35\) and check which is the first that \(24\) also divides.

Because \(24\) and \(35\) share no prime factor, a number divisible by both must carry all of \(24\)'s primes and all of \(35\)'s primes with no overlap to save on. The smallest such number is just \(24 \times 35\).
blocks.sol: The red teeth meet again at the first tooth count both gears divide evenly. Since \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\) and \(35 = 5 \times 7\) share no prime, a number divisible by both has to carry all four primes, and the smallest one that does is their product. $$24 \times 35 = \boxed{840}$$ That is \(35\) full turns of the \(24\)-tooth gear and \(24\) of the \(35\)-tooth one. Coprime numbers have nothing to share, so their lcm is just the two multiplied together.

blocks.x: That problem was the second question, the smallest count that both numbers divide evenly. When two numbers share no factors, that count is just their product. When they do share factors, it comes out smaller.
Two beacons flash every 9 seconds and every 12 seconds. List the flash times and find the first second after the start when both flash together.
hints: The first beacon flashes at the multiples of \(9\), the second at the multiples of \(12\). You want the first number that shows up on both lists of multiples.
Multiples of \(9\) are \(9, 18, 27, 36, 45, \ldots\) and multiples of \(12\) are \(12, 24, 36, 48, \ldots\). What is the smallest number appearing on both?
blocks.sol: The first beacon flashes at the multiples of \(9\) and the second at the multiples of \(12\), so walk both lists. $$9: \quad 9,\ 18,\ 27,\ 36,\ 45,\ \ldots$$ $$12: \quad 12,\ 24,\ 36,\ 48,\ \ldots$$ The first number on both is second \(\boxed{36}\), where one beacon has flashed four times and the other three. That beats \(9 \times 12 = 108\) because \(9\) and \(12\) share a factor of \(3\) that does not need counting twice.

blocks.x: Use \(168 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 7\) and \(180 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5\) to find \(\operatorname{lcm}(168, 180)\). Take each prime to its higher power, including primes in only one fingerprint.
hints: Go prime by prime again, but this time take the larger demand. For \(2\), the number \(168\) wants \(2^3\) while \(180\) only wants \(2^2\), so the lcm must supply \(2^3\) to satisfy \(168\). Do the same for every prime that appears in either number.
Every prime in either fingerprint must appear in the lcm, each to the highest power demanded by either number. Collect \(2^3\), \(3^2\), \(5\), and \(7\), then multiply.
blocks.sol: A number that both \(168\) and \(180\) divide has to meet the larger demand for every prime. For \(2\) that is \(2^3\), from \(168\). For \(3\) it is \(3^2\), from \(180\). The \(5\) and the \(7\) each show up in only one number but still have to appear. $$\operatorname{lcm}(168,180) = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 8 \times 9 \times 5 \times 7 = \boxed{2520}$$ Check that \(2520 = 168 \times 15 = 180 \times 14\). The lcm takes each prime to the higher power, the mirror of the gcd taking the lower.

blocks.x: Three subway lines depart every 12, 18, and 30 minutes. Build \(\operatorname{lcm}(12,18,30)\) from the fingerprints and report how many minutes until all three lines next leave together.
hints: Each line departs at the multiples of its own period, so all three leave together at a common multiple of \(12\), \(18\), and \(30\). You want the smallest such number, the least common multiple of all three.
Write \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), and \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\). For each prime that appears, take the highest power any of the three numbers demands, then multiply.
blocks.sol: All three lines leave together at the common multiples of \(12\), \(18\), and \(30\), so take each prime to the highest power any of the three demands. $$12 = 2^2 \times 3, \qquad 18 = 2 \times 3^2, \qquad 30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5$$ That is \(2^2\) from \(12\), \(3^2\) from \(18\), and \(5\) from \(30\). $$\operatorname{lcm}(12,18,30) = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 4 \times 9 \times 5 = \boxed{180}$$ And indeed \(180 = 12 \times 15 = 18 \times 10 = 30 \times 6\). The rule stretches to any number of values, always the highest power demanded by any of them.

blocks.x: The least common multiple lcm(a,b) is the smallest positive number that both a and b divide evenly, the smallest number that is a multiple of each. Two events repeating every a and every b steps line up exactly at the common multiples of a and b, and the first alignment is their lcm. There is no greatest common multiple, since multiples run on forever, so the least one is the only interesting extreme. Lay two fingerprints side by side and the lcm takes every prime to the higher of its two powers, because a common multiple must contain enough of every prime demanded by either number. Every prime in either fingerprint appears, and a prime in neither contributes nothing.

blocks.cap: Here are the prime fingerprints of \(168\) and \(180\) drawn as two overlapping circles. The factors they share, \(2, 2,\) and \(3\), sit in the green overlap, while \(168\) keeps an extra \(2\) and a \(7\) on its own side and \(180\) keeps an extra \(3\) and a \(5\) on its. The greatest common divisor is the product of just the shared overlap, \(2 \times 2 \times 3 = 12\), the most both numbers carry in common. The least common multiple is the product of everything across both circles, \(2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 2520\), since it must cover every prime either number demands. One picture, read two ways, the overlap for the gcd and the union for the lcm.

blocks.x: A locksmith knows two numbers have \(\gcd = 8\) and \(\operatorname{lcm} = 240\), and one number is 48. Use the relationship \(\gcd \times \operatorname{lcm} = a \times b\) to find the other number.
hints: Try multiplying a few pairs of numbers and comparing the product to the gcd times the lcm of the same pair. For example take \(12\) and \(18\): their product is \(216\), their gcd is \(6\), and their lcm is \(36\). What do you notice about \(6 \times 36\)?
For any two numbers, the gcd times the lcm equals the two numbers multiplied together. So here \(48 \times (\text{other}) = 8 \times 240\). Solve for the other number.
blocks.sol: For any pair, \(\gcd \times \operatorname{lcm} = a \times b\), so the two numbers multiply to \(8 \times 240 = 1920\). Dividing out the known one, $$\text{other} = \frac{1920}{48} = \boxed{40}$$ Checking, \(48 = 2^4 \times 3\) and \(40 = 2^3 \times 5\) share \(2^3 = 8\), and their lcm is \(2^4 \times 3 \times 5 = 240\). The rule holds because for each prime the gcd takes the lower power and the lcm takes the higher, so between them they use exactly the two powers the numbers had.

blocks.x: For any two whole numbers, gcd(a,b) × lcm(a,b) = a × b. For each prime the gcd took the lower power and the lcm took the higher power, so between them they use exactly the two powers the original numbers had, and multiplying across all primes rebuilds the pair. The most useful rearrangement is lcm(a,b) = (a × b)/(gcd(a,b)), and because of it, knowing any three of the four numbers hands you the fourth.
Dividing marbles into groups of 4, 6, or 9 always leaves exactly 1 over. What is the smallest number of marbles greater than 1 that behaves this way?
hints: If you set the one leftover marble aside, the rest divide perfectly into groups of \(4\), of \(6\), and of \(9\). So the count minus \(1\) is a common multiple of \(4\), \(6\), and \(9\).
The smallest number that \(4\), \(6\), and \(9\) all divide is \(\operatorname{lcm}(4,6,9)\). Find it, then add back the single leftover marble.
With \(4 = 2^2\), \(6 = 2 \times 3\), and \(9 = 3^2\), the lcm is \(2^2 \times 3^2 = 36\). The marble count is one more than the smallest common multiple above zero.
blocks.sol: Lift the one leftover marble away and what remains divides evenly into groups of \(4\), of \(6\), and of \(9\), so the count minus \(1\) is a common multiple of all three. $$4 = 2^2, \qquad 6 = 2 \times 3, \qquad 9 = 3^2, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(4,6,9) = 2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$$ Put the stranded marble back and the count is \(36 + 1 = \boxed{37}\). A number leaving the same remainder under several divisors sits that fixed step above a common multiple, so the smallest one is the lcm plus the remainder.

blocks.x: When a number leaves the same remainder r under several divisors, subtract r and what is left divides all of them evenly, so it is a common multiple and the smallest such number is lcm+r. When each remainder is one less than its divisor, the number sits one short of dividing cleanly, so it is one below a common multiple and the smallest is lcm-1. Either way the puzzle folds back to the multiples of a single lcm.
A bakery wants the smallest four-digit batch number divisible by 6, 8, and 9 at once. Find \(\operatorname{lcm}(6,8,9)\), then find its smallest four-digit multiple.
hints: A number divisible by \(6\), \(8\), and \(9\) is exactly a common multiple of the three, so the ones that qualify are the multiples of \(\operatorname{lcm}(6,8,9)\). Find that lcm first.
With \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(8 = 2^3\), and \(9 = 3^2\), the lcm is \(2^3 \times 3^2 = 72\). Now find the smallest four-digit multiple of \(72\) by dividing \(1000\) by \(72\) and rounding up.
blocks.sol: Divisible by \(6\), \(8\), and \(9\) at once means being a multiple of their lcm. $$6 = 2 \times 3, \qquad 8 = 2^3, \qquad 9 = 3^2, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(6,8,9) = 2^3 \times 3^2 = 72$$ Since \(1000 \div 72 \approx 13.9\), thirteen \(72\)s land at \(936\), still three digits, so the next multiple is the first to clear the line. $$72 \times 14 = \boxed{1008}$$ Hitting several divisors at once collapses the search into one list, the multiples of a single number.

blocks.x: Two pendulums swing every 21 and 28 seconds (\(21=3\times7\), \(28=2^2\times7\)). Find their lcm, then count how many times both start a swing together in the first 600 seconds.
hints: The first pendulum starts a swing at the multiples of \(21\), the second at the multiples of \(28\). They begin together exactly at the common multiples of \(21\) and \(28\), which are the multiples of \(\operatorname{lcm}(21,28)\). Find that lcm first.
With \(21 = 3 \times 7\) and \(28 = 2^2 \times 7\), the lcm is \(2^2 \times 3 \times 7 = 84\). Now count how many multiples of \(84\) land in the window from just after \(0\) up to \(600\).
Count the whole multiples of \(84\) that are at most \(600\). Since \(84 \times 7 = 588\) and \(84 \times 8 = 672\), see how many steps of \(84\) fit before passing \(600\).
blocks.sol: The pendulums start together at the common multiples of \(21\) and \(28\), which are the multiples of their lcm. $$21 = 3 \times 7, \qquad 28 = 2^2 \times 7, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(21,28) = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7 = 84$$ Stepping by \(84\) gives \(84, 168, 252, 336, 420, 504, 588\), and the next would be \(672\), past \(600\). That is \(\boxed{7}\) shared starts. Counting coincidences in a window is just counting multiples of one number, the lcm of the two periods.

blocks.x: Euclid computed gcd without factoring. Divide the larger by the smaller, keep the remainder, repeat until the remainder is zero. The last nonzero remainder is the gcd. Computers still use this today.

Both ideas come from the same two fingerprints. The overlap gives the gcd, everything across both gives the lcm, and \(\gcd\times\operatorname{lcm}=a\times b\) ties them together. The common multiples of a pair are exactly the multiples of their lcm, which sends you back to the multiple counting of 3.1.

review.x: Find \(\gcd(120, 144)\) using \(120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5\) and \(144 = 2^4 \times 3^2\). Take each shared prime to its lower power.
hints: For each prime both numbers carry, keep the lower power. For \(2\), that is \(2^3\) versus \(2^4\), so take \(2^3\). Do the same for \(3\).
Both share \(2^3\) and \(3^1\). The prime \(5\) sits only in \(120\), so it cannot join. Multiply the shared part.
review.sol: Keep each shared prime at its lower power. For \(2\) that is \(2^3\), and for \(3\) it is \(3^1\). The \(5\) appears only in \(120\), so it contributes nothing. $$\gcd(120,144) = 2^3 \times 3 = \boxed{24}$$ Check that \(120 = 24 \times 5\) and \(144 = 24 \times 6\), both whole.

review.x: Using \(120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5\) and \(144 = 2^4 \times 3^2\), find \(\operatorname{lcm}(120, 144)\) by taking each prime to its higher power.
hints: Every prime that appears in either number must appear in the lcm, each to the highest power demanded. For \(2\), take \(2^4\). For \(3\), take \(3^2\). Do not forget the \(5\).
Collect \(2^4\), \(3^2\), and \(5\), then multiply.
review.sol: Take each prime to its higher power, including one carried by just a single number. For \(2\) that is \(2^4\), for \(3\) it is \(3^2\), and the \(5\) from \(120\) has to come along. $$\operatorname{lcm}(120,144) = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 16 \times 9 \times 5 = \boxed{720}$$ The gcd was \(24\), and \(24 \times 720 = 17280 = 120 \times 144\), exactly as \(\gcd \times \operatorname{lcm} = a \times b\) promises.

review.x: With \(49 = 7^2\) and \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\), do these numbers share any prime factor? Report their greatest common divisor.
hints: Look at the two fingerprints. Do they have any prime in common at all? If not, the only number dividing both is \(1\).
\(49\) is built only from \(7\), while \(60\) is built from \(2\), \(3\), and \(5\). No prime is shared.
review.sol: \(49 = 7^2\) is built only from \(7\), and \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\) carries no \(7\) at all. With no prime in common, the only number dividing both is \(\boxed{1}\). Two numbers that share no prime are called coprime, and their gcd is always \(1\).

review.x: Two numbers have \(\gcd = 9\) and \(\operatorname{lcm} = 270\). One number is 45. Find the other.
hints: The gcd times the lcm equals the two numbers multiplied together. So \(45 \times (\text{other}) = 9 \times 270\).
Compute \(9 \times 270 = 2430\), then divide by \(45\).
review.sol: Since \(\gcd \times \operatorname{lcm} = a \times b\), the two numbers multiply to \(9 \times 270 = 2430\). Dividing out the known one, $$\text{other} = \frac{2430}{45} = \boxed{54}$$ Checking, \(45 = 3^2 \times 5\) and \(54 = 2 \times 3^3\) share \(3^2 = 9\), and their lcm is \(2 \times 3^3 \times 5 = 270\).

review.x: Two ferries leave together and return every 16 and 24 minutes. How many minutes until both depart together again?
hints: Each ferry departs at the multiples of its own period, so they leave together at the common multiples of \(16\) and \(24\). You want the least common multiple.
With \(16 = 2^4\) and \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), take each prime to its higher power.
review.sol: The ferries leave together at the common multiples of \(16\) and \(24\), and the first one is their lcm. $$16 = 2^4, \qquad 24 = 2^3 \times 3, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(16,24) = 2^4 \times 3 = \boxed{48}$$ Check that \(48 = 16 \times 3 = 24 \times 2\), both whole.

review.x: Stacking badges leaves 1 over for groups of 5, 6, or 8. What is the smallest badge count greater than 1 with this property?
hints: Set the single leftover badge aside, and the rest divide perfectly into stacks of \(5\), \(6\), and \(8\). So the count minus \(1\) is a common multiple of all three.
Find \(\operatorname{lcm}(5,6,8)\), then add back the one leftover badge.
review.sol: Set the leftover badge aside and the rest divides evenly into stacks of \(5\), \(6\), and \(8\), so the count minus \(1\) is a common multiple of the three. With \(6 = 2 \times 3\) and \(8 = 2^3\), $$\operatorname{lcm}(5,6,8) = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 120.$$ Adding the badge back gives \(120 + 1 = \boxed{121}\). Check that \(121 = 5 \times 24 + 1 = 6 \times 20 + 1 = 8 \times 15 + 1\).

review.x: Two readings of two fingerprints. The gcd takes each shared prime to its lower power, and the lcm takes every prime to its higher power. They satisfy \(\gcd\times\operatorname{lcm}=a\times b\). Common multiples are multiples of the lcm.
Two rhythms of 9 and 12 beats loop together. Find the largest common multiple of 9 and 12 below 300.
hints: A length that is a whole number of repeats of both rhythms is a common multiple of \(9\) and \(12\), which means a multiple of \(\operatorname{lcm}(9,12)\). Find that lcm first.
Since \(\operatorname{lcm}(9,12) = 36\), the common multiples are \(36, 72, 108, \ldots\). Find the largest one under \(300\).
review.sol: A loop that is a whole number of both rhythms is a common multiple of \(9\) and \(12\), so it is a multiple of their lcm. $$9 = 3^2, \qquad 12 = 2^2 \times 3, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(9,12) = 2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$$ Since \(300 \div 36 \approx 8.3\), the largest multiple staying under \(300\) is \(36 \times 8 = \boxed{288}\), and the next one, \(324\), sails past. The common multiples of two numbers are exactly the multiples of their lcm, so a hunt like this only ever scans one list.

review.x: A poster shop prints only in runs divisible by 4, 5, and 6 at once. Find \(\operatorname{lcm}(4,5,6)\) and its smallest three-digit multiple.
hints: A run divisible by \(4\), \(5\), and \(6\) at once is a multiple of their least common multiple. Find \(\operatorname{lcm}(4,5,6)\) first.
With \(4 = 2^2\), \(5 = 5\), and \(6 = 2 \times 3\), the lcm is \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60\). The smallest three-digit multiple of \(60\) is the next one after \(60\) itself.
review.sol: A run divisible by all three is a common multiple of \(4\), \(5\), and \(6\), so it is a multiple of their lcm. $$4 = 2^2, \qquad 5 = 5, \qquad 6 = 2 \times 3, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(4,5,6) = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$$ The multiples of \(60\) run \(60, 120, 180, \ldots\), and the first with three digits is \(\boxed{120}\). Check that \(120 = 4 \times 30 = 5 \times 24 = 6 \times 20\).

review.x: Two lights flash every 10 and 15 seconds. In 300 seconds after the start, how many times do both flash together?
hints: The lights flash together at the common multiples of \(10\) and \(15\), which are the multiples of \(\operatorname{lcm}(10,15)\). Find that lcm.
Since \(\operatorname{lcm}(10,15) = 30\), count how many multiples of \(30\) fall in the \(300\) seconds after the start.
review.sol: The lights coincide at the common multiples of \(10\) and \(15\), which are the multiples of their lcm. $$10 = 2 \times 5, \qquad 15 = 3 \times 5, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(10,15) = 2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30$$ So they flash together every \(30\) seconds, and \(300 \div 30 = \boxed{10}\) of those land in the window, at \(30, 60, 90\), on up to \(300\).

review.x: A crowd leaves 1 person over for teams of 2, 3, 4, or 5. What is the smallest crowd greater than 1 with this property?
hints: Set the one leftover person aside, and the rest split evenly into teams of \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), and \(5\). So the crowd minus \(1\) is a common multiple of all four.
Find \(\operatorname{lcm}(2,3,4,5)\), then add back the single leftover person.
review.sol: Set the leftover person aside and the rest splits evenly into teams of \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), and \(5\), so the crowd minus \(1\) is a common multiple of all four. $$\operatorname{lcm}(2,3,4,5) = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$$ Adding that person back gives \(60 + 1 = \boxed{61}\). Check that \(61\) leaves exactly \(1\) over for each of the four team sizes.

review.x: A wall is 132 cm by 198 cm. Using \(132 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 11\) and \(198 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 11\), find the side length of the largest square tile that fits exactly.
hints: A square tile of side \(s\) fits the wall exactly only if \(s\) divides both the width \(132\) and the height \(198\) with nothing left over. So \(s\) is a common divisor, and you want the greatest.
Take each shared prime to its lower power. Both numbers carry \(2\), \(3\), and \(11\), though to different powers.
review.sol: A tile of side \(s\) fits exactly only when \(s\) divides both \(132\) and \(198\), so the largest tile is the gcd. Each shared prime goes to its lower power, giving one \(2\), one \(3\), and one \(11\). $$\gcd(132,198) = 2 \times 3 \times 11 = \boxed{66}$$ The tile is \(66\) cm on a side, fitting \(2\) across and \(3\) up. The largest square that tiles a whole-number rectangle is always the gcd of the two sides.

review.x: A number leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, remainder 5 when divided by 6, and remainder 7 when divided by 8. Notice each remainder is one less than its divisor. What is the smallest such number?
hints: Compare each remainder to its divisor. \(3\) is one less than \(4\), \(5\) is one less than \(6\), and \(7\) is one less than \(8\). So the number is one short of dividing each evenly.
If the number were one larger, it would divide evenly by \(4\), \(6\), and \(8\), making it a common multiple. So the number is \(\operatorname{lcm}(4,6,8) - 1\).
review.sol: Each remainder is one less than its divisor, so adding \(1\) would make the number divide evenly by \(4\), \(6\), and \(8\) at once. That puts it one below a common multiple. $$4 = 2^2, \qquad 6 = 2 \times 3, \qquad 8 = 2^3, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(4,6,8) = 2^3 \times 3 = 24$$ So the number is \(24 - 1 = \boxed{23}\). Check that \(23 = 4 \times 5 + 3 = 6 \times 3 + 5 = 8 \times 2 + 7\).

review.x: GCD and LCM are the engines of fractions. Reducing divides by the gcd, and adding different-denominator fractions uses the lcm as common denominator. Master these now and fraction work becomes routine.

blocks.x: Lesson 3.1 found that perfect squares alone have an odd divisor count. Lesson 3.3 gave every number a unique prime fingerprint. Now we count a number's divisors straight from that fingerprint, without listing a single one.
A machine builds divisors of \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\) by choosing how many 2s (0, 1, or 2) and how many 3s (0 or 1) to multiply together. How many different divisors can it build?
hints: You make two separate choices, the number of \(2\)s (three options) and the number of \(3\)s (two options). Every pairing of one choice with the other gives a divisor. Count the pairings.
Three options for the \(2\)s and two options for the \(3\)s give \(3 \times 2\) combinations. List them as \(2^i \times 3^j\) and confirm you get \(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12\).
blocks.sol: The \(2\)s can appear \(0\), \(1\), or \(2\) times, which is three choices, and the \(3\) can appear \(0\) or \(1\) times, which is two. The choices are independent, so the divisors number $$3 \times 2 = \boxed{6}.$$ Listing them as \(2^i \times 3^j\) gives \(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12\), exactly six. Each prime offers one more choice than its exponent, and independent choices multiply.

blocks.x: Add-one-and-multiply rule. If $n = p^a \times q^b \times \cdots$, the number of positive divisors is $(a+1)(b+1)\cdots$. Every divisor is built by choosing how many copies of each prime to take, from $0$ up to that prime power, so a prime with exponent $a$ offers $a+1$ choices. The choices are independent, so they multiply, and that single product counts every divisor at once.

blocks.cap: The rule becomes a picture for \(72 = 2^3 \times 3^2\). Each divisor picks one power of \(2\) for its column, from \(2^0\) up to \(2^3\), giving four columns, and one power of \(3\) for its row, from \(3^0\) up to \(3^2\), giving three rows. Every cell of the grid is one divisor, the product of its row and column headers, so the divisors fill a tidy \(4 \times 3\) rectangle. That is why the count is \((3+1)(2+1) = 12\), the same as adding one to each exponent and multiplying. The two green cells, \(9\) and \(36\), are the divisors that happen to be perfect squares themselves, a hint of something we will return to in a moment.

blocks.x: The fingerprint of 360 is \(360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5\). Use the add-one-and-multiply rule to count how many positive divisors 360 has without listing them.
hints: Each prime contributes one more choice than its exponent. The prime \(2\) has exponent \(3\), so it offers \(3 + 1\) choices. Do the same for \(3\) and for \(5\), then multiply.
The choice counts are \(3+1 = 4\) for the \(2\)s, \(2+1 = 3\) for the \(3\)s, and \(1+1 = 2\) for the \(5\). Multiply \(4 \times 3 \times 2\).
blocks.sol: Add one to each exponent and multiply. $$(3+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 4 \times 3 \times 2 = \boxed{24}.$$ So \(360\) has \(24\) positive divisors, found without writing one of them down. The rule handles as many primes as a number carries, turning a long listing chore into a single multiplication.

blocks.x: Compare \(96 = 2^5 \times 3\) and \(100 = 2^2 \times 5^2\). Apply the counting rule to each. Which number has more divisors?
hints: Apply add-one-and-multiply to each. For \(96 = 2^5 \times 3\), the counts are \(5+1\) and \(1+1\). For \(100 = 2^2 \times 5^2\), the counts are \(2+1\) and \(2+1\).
\(96\) gives \(6 \times 2 = 12\) divisors, while \(100\) gives \(3 \times 3 = 9\). Which is larger?
blocks.sol: For \(96 = 2^5 \times 3\), the count is $$(5+1)(1+1) = 6 \times 2 = 12.$$ For \(100 = 2^2 \times 5^2\), it is $$(2+1)(2+1) = 3 \times 3 = 9.$$ The bigger number has fewer divisors, so the answer is \(\boxed{96}\). Divisor count follows the shape of the exponents, not the size of the number. One tall stack of \(2\)s beats two medium stacks here.

blocks.x: The divisor count \((a+1)(b+1)\cdots\) is odd only when every exponent is even, the fingerprint of a perfect square. How many numbers from 1 to 50 have an odd number of divisors?
hints: The divisor count is a product \((a+1)(b+1)\cdots\). A product of whole numbers is odd only when every single factor in it is odd. So ask, when is every \(a+1\) odd?
Every \(a+1\) is odd exactly when every exponent \(a\) is even, which is precisely when the number is a perfect square. So count the perfect squares from \(1\) to \(50\).
blocks.sol: A product of whole numbers is odd only when every factor is odd, and \(a+1\) is odd exactly when \(a\) is even. So an odd divisor count means every exponent is even, which is the fingerprint of a perfect square. From \(1\) to \(50\) the squares are $$1,\ 4,\ 9,\ 16,\ 25,\ 36,\ 49,$$ the squares of \(1\) through \(7\), since \(8^2 = 64\) overshoots. That is \(\boxed{7}\) numbers. This is lesson 3.1's result again, now falling straight out of the counting rule.

blocks.x: A number has an odd number of divisors exactly when it is a perfect square. From 3.1, only a perfect square has a factor that pairs with itself, leaving one unpaired. From the counting rule, the product $(a+1)(b+1)\cdots$ is odd only when every exponent is even, which is the fingerprint of a perfect square. The pairing argument and the counting rule land in the same place.
Find the smallest whole number with exactly 12 divisors by breaking 12 into exponent-plus-one pieces, building the smallest number from each, and comparing.
hints: You need \((a+1)(b+1)\cdots = 12\). The ways to write \(12\) as such a product include \(12\), \(6 \times 2\), \(4 \times 3\), and \(3 \times 2 \times 2\). Each gives a set of exponents to spend on primes.

To keep the number small, give the biggest exponents to the smallest primes. For the split \(3 \times 2 \times 2\), that means \(2^2 \times 3^1 \times 5^1\). Build the number for each split and take the least.
Compare \(2^{11} = 2048\), \(2^5 \times 3 = 96\), \(2^3 \times 3^2 = 72\), and \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60\). Which is smallest?
blocks.sol: The exponent-plus-one values have to multiply to \(12\), and to keep the number small the biggest exponents go on the smallest primes. $$12 = 12 \ \Rightarrow\ 2^{11} = 2048$$ $$12 = 6 \times 2 \ \Rightarrow\ 2^{5} \times 3 = 96$$ $$12 = 4 \times 3 \ \Rightarrow\ 2^{3} \times 3^{2} = 72$$ $$12 = 3 \times 2 \times 2 \ \Rightarrow\ 2^{2} \times 3 \times 5 = 60$$ The smallest is \(\boxed{60}\). Spreading the choices across \(2, 3, 5\) is cheaper than stacking them all on \(2\).

blocks.x: \(720=2^4\times3^2\times5\). An even divisor must contain at least one 2. How many even divisors does 720 have?
hints: An even divisor must take at least one \(2\). Normally the \(2\)s offer choices \(0, 1, 2, 3, 4\), but forbidding zero \(2\)s leaves only \(1, 2, 3, 4\). The \(3\)s and the \(5\) keep all their choices.
So the even divisors number \(4 \times (2+1) \times (1+1)\). Alternatively, count all the divisors and subtract the odd ones, which are the divisors of \(3^2 \times 5\).
blocks.sol: An even divisor of \(720 = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5\) must take at least one \(2\), so the \(2\)s drop from five choices to the four \(1, 2, 3, 4\). The \(3\)s still give \(2+1 = 3\) and the \(5\) gives \(1+1 = 2\), so the even divisors number $$4 \times 3 \times 2 = \boxed{24}.$$ Restricting one prime's choices counts a whole family of divisors directly. Cross-check, \(720\) has \(30\) divisors and \(6\) odd ones, and \(30 - 6 = 24\).

blocks.x: Highly composite numbers beat every smaller number in divisor count: 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24, 36, 60, 120, 360. Civilizations pick these for time and angles because many divisors make sharing easy.

Every tool in this chapter came from the same move. Find a number's primes, read the fingerprint, and divisibility, perfect powers, GCD, LCM, and the exact divisor count all follow. Chapter 4 turns to fractions.

review.x: A number is given as \(2^4 \times 5^2\). Use the add-one-and-multiply rule to count its positive divisors.
hints: Add one to each exponent and multiply. The \(2\)s give \(4+1\) choices and the \(5\)s give \(2+1\).
review.sol: Add one to each exponent and multiply. $$(4+1)(2+1) = 5 \times 3 = \boxed{15}.$$ The divisors are \(2^i \times 5^j\) with \(i\) from \(0\) to \(4\) and \(j\) from \(0\) to \(2\), which is \(5\) by \(3\) pairs.

review.x: Factor \(600 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5^2\) and apply the counting rule. How many positive divisors does 600 have?
hints: With \(600 = 2^3 \times 3^1 \times 5^2\), the choice counts are \(3+1\), \(1+1\), and \(2+1\).
Multiply \(4 \times 2 \times 3\).
review.sol: Reading the fingerprint \(600 = 2^3 \times 3^1 \times 5^2\), $$(3+1)(1+1)(2+1) = 4 \times 2 \times 3 = \boxed{24}.$$ Once a number is in fingerprint form, its divisor count is one multiplication away.

review.x: Which has more divisors, \(64 = 2^6\) or \(90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5\)? Count each and enter the number with more.
hints: \(64\) gives \(7\) divisors, while \(90\) gives \(2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12\). Which is larger?
review.sol: For \(64 = 2^6\), the count is \(6+1 = 7\). For \(90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5\), it is \((1+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12\). So \(\boxed{90}\) has more, twelve against seven. Spreading primes out makes far more divisors than stacking one prime high, so the count tracks fingerprint shape, not size.

review.x: How many whole numbers from 1 to 100 have an odd number of divisors?
hints: A number has an odd divisor count exactly when it is a perfect square, since that forces every exponent even. So count the perfect squares from \(1\) to \(100\).
The perfect squares are \(1, 4, 9, \ldots, 100\), the squares of \(1\) through \(10\).
review.sol: A divisor count is odd only when every exponent is even, which means the number is a perfect square. From \(1\) to \(100\) those are $$1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100,$$ the squares of \(1\) through \(10\), so the answer is \(\boxed{10}\). Odd divisor counts belong to perfect squares and nothing else, so counting them is just counting squares.

review.x: Find the smallest whole number with exactly 8 divisors.
hints: You need \((a+1)(b+1)\cdots = 8\). The ways include \(8\), \(4 \times 2\), and \(2 \times 2 \times 2\), giving exponent sets \(\{7\}\), \(\{3,1\}\), and \(\{1,1,1\}\).
Put the biggest exponents on the smallest primes. Compare \(2^7 = 128\), \(2^3 \times 3 = 24\), and \(2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30\).
review.sol: The exponent-plus-one values must multiply to \(8\), and the biggest exponents go on the smallest primes. $$8 = 8 \ \Rightarrow\ 2^7 = 128, \qquad 8 = 4 \times 2 \ \Rightarrow\ 2^3 \times 3 = 24, \qquad 8 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \ \Rightarrow\ 2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30.$$ The smallest is \(\boxed{24}\), whose divisors are \(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24\).

review.x: How many positive divisors does \(2^{10}\) have?
hints: A power of a single prime, \(p^a\), has its divisors \(p^0, p^1, \ldots, p^a\). How many is that?
The exponent runs from \(0\) up to \(10\), so add one to the exponent.
review.sol: The divisors of \(2^{10}\) are \(2^0, 2^1, \ldots, 2^{10}\), one for each exponent from \(0\) to \(10\), so there are \(10 + 1 = \boxed{11}\). A prime raised to the power \(a\) has \(a+1\) divisors, the simplest case of the rule.

review.x: A number has exactly three divisors only when it is the square of a prime. How many numbers from 1 to 50 have exactly three divisors?
hints: For the divisor count \((a+1)(b+1)\cdots\) to equal \(3\), and since \(3\) is prime, the product must be a single factor \(3\). That means one prime with exponent \(2\) and no others.
So the number must be the square of a prime, \(p^2\). List the prime squares up to \(50\).
review.sol: For \((a+1)(b+1)\cdots\) to equal \(3\), and \(3\) is prime, the product must be the single factor \(3\). That forces one prime with exponent \(2\) and nothing else, so the number is a prime squared. Up to \(50\) those are $$2^2 = 4,\quad 3^2 = 9,\quad 5^2 = 25,\quad 7^2 = 49,$$ since \(11^2 = 121\) overshoots. That is \(\boxed{4}\) numbers. The divisors of \(p^2\) are just \(1\), \(p\), and \(p^2\), which is why three divisors always means a prime square.

review.x: How many of 360's divisors are even, given \(360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5\)?
hints: An even divisor must take at least one \(2\), so the \(2\)s offer choices \(1, 2, 3\) instead of \(0, 1, 2, 3\). That is \(3\) choices. The \(3\)s and the \(5\) keep their full counts.
Even divisors number \(3 \times (2+1) \times (1+1)\). Or count all \(24\) divisors and subtract the odd ones, the divisors of \(3^2 \times 5\).
review.sol: An even divisor needs at least one \(2\), so the \(2\)s drop from four choices to the three \(1, 2, 3\). The \(3\)s give \(2+1 = 3\) and the \(5\) gives \(1+1 = 2\), so the even divisors number $$3 \times 3 \times 2 = \boxed{18}.$$ Cross-check, \(360\) has \(24\) divisors and \(6\) odd ones, the divisors of \(3^2 \times 5\), and \(24 - 6 = 18\).

review.x: Divisor counting rule. For \(n=p^a q^b\cdots\), count is \((a+1)(b+1)\cdots\). Depends on exponent shape, not size. Odd count ↔ perfect square. Trim one prime's choices for a sub-family. Run backward to design a number with a target count.
Locker \(n\) is flipped once per divisor, so it ends open only when it has an odd divisor count, exactly the perfect squares. Open lockers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.

blocks.x: Chapter 3 looked inside numbers for factors and ended with a master key, the prime fingerprint. Factors set the stage, divisibility tests gave quick eyes, primes were atoms, and GCD, LCM, and divisor counts all followed.

Factors and multiples are one relationship read from two ends. A factor of \(n\) is a side of a rectangle of area \(n\), so factors arrive in pairs that multiply to \(n\), \(d\) with its partner \(n \div d\). Turn the arrow around and the small number is a factor while the large one is a multiple. From this came several facts. A number has finitely many factors but infinitely many multiples, \(1\) divides everything, every number is both a factor and a multiple of itself, and \(0\) is a multiple of every number. And a number has an odd factor count exactly when it is a perfect square, the lone case where a factor pairs with itself.

Closure and chaining. Add or subtract two multiples of \(n\) and you land on a multiple of \(n\) again, since the shared \(n\) factors out, so a stray non-multiple can never be added onto a multiple to reach one. That is closure. And if \(a\) is a factor of \(b\), then every multiple of \(b\) is automatically a multiple of \(a\), since the multiple carries \(b\) inside it and \(b\) carries \(a\). That is chaining, and it runs only downward toward the smaller factors. These two ideas powered every divisibility test that followed.

With that structure in hand, the next question was practical. Must you divide a big number out the long way to know whether some small number goes into it, or can you glance at the digits and simply know? Place value gave the answer.

Divisibility tests all spring from place value. Cut a number where one chunk becomes a multiple of the divisor, let closure throw that chunk away, and judge the small piece left behind. The last digit settles \(2\), \(5\), \(10\), since every higher place is a multiple of ten. The last two digits settle \(4\) and the last three settle \(8\), since \(100 = 4 \times 25\) and \(1000 = 8 \times 125\). The digit sum settles \(9\) and \(3\), since every power of ten is one above a run of nines. The alternating digit sum settles \(11\), since the powers of ten bounce just below then above its multiples. Run any test backward and the same cut recovers a hidden digit.

Combine tests only along coprime factors. Split a composite divisor into coprime parts and test each. A split like \(12 = 2 \times 6\) fails because 2 and 6 share a factor, so passing both tests would count that shared factor twice while 12 demands it twice.
Testing for small factors led naturally to the smallest building blocks of all, the numbers that have no factors to find.

Primes are the atoms. A prime has exactly two divisors, a composite has more, 1 is neither, and 2 is the only even prime. To test primality, divide by primes up to \(\sqrt{n}\) and stop, any factor above \(\sqrt{n}\) has a smaller partner already checked.

Every number has one unique prime fingerprint (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic). Written with exponents like \(360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5\), it reveals: perfect square ↔ all exponents even, perfect cube ↔ all multiples of 3, trailing zeros = count of 2-and-5 pairs. Primes never run out.
Once a single number could be broken into its atoms, two numbers could be compared atom by atom, which opened the last ideas of the chapter.

GCD and LCM are two readings of two fingerprints. GCD takes each shared prime to its lower power. LCM takes every prime to its higher power. They satisfy \(\gcd\times\operatorname{lcm}=a\times b\). Numbers sharing no prime are coprime, and common multiples of a pair are multiples of their lcm.

The fingerprint counts divisors too. For \(n = p^a q^b \cdots\), the divisor count is \((a+1)(b+1)\cdots\). It depends on exponent shape, not size, so a smaller number can out-divide a larger one. The count is odd exactly for perfect squares.

The prime fingerprint settled divisibility, perfect powers, GCD, LCM, and divisor counts throughout the chapter. Chapter 4 turns to fractions, and these tools come straight along: GCD reduces fractions, LCM gives common denominators.
